implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits whichever platform it runs on, and both mainstream ones provide the structure. On Ktor the Routing plugin supplies the transport - routing { get("healthz") { call.respondText("ok") } } - so only the check set, the status mapping (call.respond(HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable, ...)) and a cached aggregate remain; on Spring Boot the surface is the same Actuator health endpoint and health groups as in Java, declared with Kotlin beans and properties. The classic registry is justified when several checks must be aggregated under per-check deadlines, and the runtime choice should follow the framework the service already uses rather than the pattern.
idiom_name: Ktor route handler (or Spring Boot Actuator under Kotlin)
pitfalls: A blocking check (plain JDBC, file I/O) called straight from a coroutine handler occupies a dispatcher thread - wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) and withTimeout, otherwise the probe starves the event loop it is measuring.
A health route contributed by a Ktor plugin/module that is not installed in every environment silently disappears, so the probe fails for a deployment reason rather than an application fault.

Under Spring Boot, readiness and liveness groups are configuration: enabling probes without adding the intended indicators to the readiness group yields a green liveness and a meaningless readiness endpoint.
